title: Where should you store JWT in the browser: HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie (safest) vs localStorage (vulnerable to XSS) vs sessionStorage: and why?
shortTitle: Where to Store JWT in the Browser (HttpOnly Cookie vs localStorage vs sessionStorage)
keyPoints: HttpOnly cookie: JavaScript cannot read it, so XSS cannot steal the token; the safest browser storage for JWTs.
Secure flag: the cookie is only sent over HTTPS, preventing interception on plain HTTP.
SameSite attribute: Strict or Lax prevents the cookie from being sent on cross-site requests, blocking CSRF.
localStorage: persists across tabs and restarts, but readable by any JavaScript, so one XSS means full token theft.
sessionStorage: scoped to one tab and cleared on close, slightly reducing exposure, but still XSS-vulnerable.
For SPAs that must use header-based tokens, keep the access token in memory only and the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie.

s1_definition.oneliner: Prefer an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie so JavaScript cannot steal the token; localStorage is one XSS away from losing everything.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **HttpOnly cookie** – the server sets the cookie with the `HttpOnly` flag, making it invisible to `document.cookie` and all JavaScript; this is the safest storage for browser-based JWTs.
- **Secure flag** – ensures the cookie is only transmitted over HTTPS, preventing interception on plain HTTP.
- **SameSite attribute** – `Strict` or `Lax` prevents the browser from attaching the cookie to cross-site requests, blocking most CSRF attacks.
- **localStorage** – a JavaScript-accessible key-value store that persists across tabs and restarts; readable by any script, so one XSS flaw leaks the token.
- **sessionStorage** – scoped to one tab and cleared on close; still fully readable by JavaScript, so XSS risk remains.
s1_definition.analogy: Storing a JWT in localStorage is like leaving Rajesh's cheque book on the open counter of National Bank of India: any clerk (any script) passing by can grab it. Storing it in an HttpOnly cookie is like keeping the cheque book in a sealed drawer that only the bank's own back-office machinery can open; the counter staff and visitors cannot reach inside. The sealed drawer is safer, but because it opens automatically for every transaction, the bank adds a second check (SameSite and CSRF tokens) so a trickster cannot make the drawer open for the wrong request.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  localStorage (DANGEROUS):
  ┌──────────────┐      ┌───────────────┐
  │  JavaScript  │ ────►│ localStorage  │
  │  (any script)│ read │  jwt=eyJhb... │
  │              │◄──── │               │
  │  XSS steals  │      └───────────────┘
  │  the token!  │
  └──────────────┘

  HttpOnly Cookie (SAFE):
  ┌──────────────┐      ┌───────────────┐
  │  JavaScript  │ ──X──│ HttpOnly      │
  │  (any script)│ BLOCK│ Cookie        │
  │              │      │ jwt=eyJhb...  │
  │  CANNOT read │      └───────┬───────┘
  └──────────────┘              │
                                │ auto-attached
                                ▼
                        ┌───────────────┐
                        │  Server       │
                        │  reads cookie │
                        └───────────────┘
```

```text
  SPA Recommended Pattern:
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │   Browser (SPA)  │
  │                  │
  │  Access Token:   │  ◄── in-memory variable (JS)
  │  let at = "..."; │      lost on refresh (safe)
  │                  │
  │  Refresh Token:  │  ◄── HttpOnly cookie
  │  (invisible to   │      scoped to /auth/refresh
  │   JavaScript)    │
  └────────┬─────────┘
           │
           │ AT expired? Call /auth/refresh
           │ Browser auto-sends RT cookie
           ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │   Auth Server    │
  │  Validates RT    │
  │  Issues new AT   │ ──► returned in body
  │  Rotates RT      │ ──► new HttpOnly cookie
  └──────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The safest place to keep a JWT in a browser is an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. HttpOnly means JavaScript cannot read the cookie through document.cookie, so even a successful cross-site scripting attack cannot steal the token. Secure means the cookie only travels over HTTPS. SameSite, set to Strict or Lax, means the browser will not attach the cookie to requests that originate from other sites, which blocks the classic CSRF attack. Storing the token in localStorage or sessionStorage instead makes it readable by any script on the page, so a single XSS flaw hands the attacker the token.

In the National Bank of India project, this distinction is critical because the blast radius of a stolen token is full account access. With localStorage a simulated malicious script reads the token in one line, which in the real world means account takeover. With the HttpOnly cookie the same script gets nothing because the browser hides it from JavaScript.

The trade-off is that cookies are sent automatically, which is convenient but opens CSRF. SameSite closes that by refusing to send the cookie on cross-site requests, and for sensitive state-changing endpoints a CSRF token is added for defense in depth. localStorage avoids CSRF because the app attaches the token manually, but that is a poor consolation because XSS is far more common and far more damaging.

For SPAs that must use header-based tokens, the recommendation is to keep the access token only in a JavaScript variable in memory, which is lost on refresh and never persisted, and keep the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie. For native mobile apps, tokens go in the platform secure storage like Keychain or Keystore.

Remember one sentence: store tokens in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies so JavaScript cannot steal them, and treat localStorage as one XSS away from full account takeover.
